questions.text: For a perfectly normal distribution, approximately what percentage of observations fall OUTSIDE the IQR-rule fences (Q1 − 1.5×IQR and Q3 + 1.5×IQR)?
options: About 5%
About 1%
About 0.7%
About 0.1%
questions.explanation: For a normal distribution, the IQR fences correspond to approximately μ ± 2.7σ, which contains about 99.3% of observations. So about 0.7% of genuinely normal data falls outside the fences — a low false-positive rate.

questions.text: You want to detect outliers in a right-skewed distribution where the standard deviation is large due to the outliers themselves. Which method is MORE robust?
options: Z-score, because it standardises the data
IQR rule, because it uses quantiles that are not affected by extreme values
Z-score, because it uses both the mean and standard deviation
Neither method works for skewed data
questions.explanation: The IQR rule uses Q1 and Q3 (medians of the lower and upper halves), which are resistant to extreme values. The Z-score uses the mean and standard deviation, which are both inflated by the very outliers you are trying to detect — making Z-score less reliable for skewed data.

questions.text: Winsorisation at the 1st/99th percentile replaces extreme values with:
options: The mean of the column
Zero
The value at the 1st or 99th percentile (whichever fence is crossed)
A randomly imputed value from the observed distribution
questions.explanation: Winsorisation caps values: anything below p1 is set to p1, anything above p99 is set to p99. Values within the fences are unchanged. This retains all records but limits the leverage of extreme values.

questions.text: Why do we use log(x + 1) rather than log(x) when transforming claim_amount?
options: Adding 1 makes the log values positive
claim_amount can be zero (no claim filed), and log(0) is undefined (-∞)
The +1 correction removes outliers from the upper tail
log(x) is only valid for values greater than 100
questions.explanation: When a variable can take the value zero, log(0) = −∞, which breaks arithmetic. Adding 1 shifts all values up by 1 so that the minimum becomes log(1) = 0. For large values, the +1 has negligible effect.

questions.text: Deleting all rows that contain an outlier is generally the safest treatment for outliers in a large dataset.
questions.explanation: Deleting outliers removes records, reducing sample size and potentially introducing bias — particularly if outliers are informative (e.g., genuinely high claims or fraudulent transactions). Winsorisation or transformation are usually preferred because they retain the records.

questions.text: In OLS regression, a single outlier can disproportionately influence the fitted coefficients because:
options: OLS minimises the sum of squared residuals, so large deviations are penalised quadratically
OLS minimises the sum of absolute residuals, making it sensitive to any deviation
OLS excludes the median from its calculation
Outliers always have high leverage regardless of their position on the x-axis
questions.explanation: OLS minimises the sum of SQUARED residuals. Squaring amplifies large errors: an observation with a residual of 10 contributes 100 to the loss, while one with residual 1 contributes only 1. This quadratic penalty means outliers exert disproportionate influence on the fitted line.
